extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and first-aid rules for prevention and immediate treatment of food-borne parasites, insect bites and stings, animal bites, snake bites, burns, scalds, and frostbite intended for non-specialist caregivers. Covers recognition, immediate steps, home remedies, and when to seek or defer to professional care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk pasteurization for children's consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless all doubt has been removed, it is best to subject milk intended for children's consumption to a temperature of 160 deg. F. for ten minutes, and then put it on the ice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only clean, pure milk free from bacteria; do not use partially or entirely soured milk except for cooked preparations. Heating to 160°F for 10 minutes renders germs harmless while preserving nourishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing food parasites by thorough cooking
rubrics_metrics.description: The entrance of living food parasites can be absolutely prevented by thorough cooking of meats, especially pork and beef. Heat destroys the 'measles' and the trichina worms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parasites discussed include echinococcus, guineaworm, hookworm, trichina, and tapeworm. Some (e.g., echinococcus) cannot be diagnosed by the layman; prevention via thorough cooking is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tapeworm (measly meat) recognition and deworming remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tapeworm infection follows eating 'measly' beef or pork; sections of the worm often appear in stool. When no physician is available, after fasting 24 hours, take pumpkin seed (outer coverings removed) soaked overnight and taken on an empty stomach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dosage: child 1–2 ounces mashed with syrup/honey; adult 4 ounces. Treatment is ideally directed by a physician. Symptoms include vertigo, dyspepsia, emaciation; diagnosis often by passage of worm segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichiniasis — prevention and prognosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Trichiniasis is caused by trichinae from raw or partly cooked pork, ham, or bacon; early symptoms include nausea, vomiting, colic, and diarrhea; later muscular stiffness and systemic signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no specific treatment described; prevention by thoroughly cooking pork is essential. Many non-fatal cases may be misdiagnosed as rheumatism; some pneumonia cases may be caused by trichinae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potato poisoning (solanine) prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Solanine is developed in potatoes especially during sprouting and can cause violent vomiting and diarrhea and inflammation of the stomach and bowels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful peeling of sprouting potatoes and removal of their eyes lessens or may obviate danger. This poisoning is considered rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosquito-borne disease prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent malaria and yellow fever, mosquito bites must be prevented by nettings in houses and breeding places destroyed (drain pools, ponds, marshes); petroleum (kerosene) may be poured on surface waters to arrest larvae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish Anopheles (malaria vector) vs Culex (common house mosquito) by palpi, wing markings, posture, and breeding habitats. Prevention targets vector control and physical barriers (nets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of mosquito and similar insect bites
rubrics_metrics.description: All poisons introduced into the body by insects are of an acid nature; the best remedy is an alkali. Dip clean hands in hot water with dissolved carbolic acid or use a kerosene/water mixture, rub on exposed skin while wet, then allow to dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific topical alkali remedies: diluted ammonia (water of ammonia) or a strong solution of saleratus/baking soda in water applied by bathing or on cloths. Mud (clean clay + water) poultice is also useful in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bee, wasp, and hornet sting management
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract the sting of bees before all the poison has come away (forceps or pressing a small key tube over the puncture). Ammonia water is recommended to relieve pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bee stings are barbed and remain, whereas wasps/hornets can sting repeatedly. Bee-keepers may develop immunity. Prompt removal and alkali application are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wood tick removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove ticks by painting them with turpentine to kill or relax them so they drop off; if a tropical variety buries its head and turpentine fails, the head must be dug out with a clean needle or knife blade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tick bites are largely painless until engorged; removing the proboscis left in the skin is important to prevent painful local suppuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head lice — recognition and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Head lice cause itching (esp. lower back of head) with nits glued to hair. Treatment: cut hair when permissible; soften crusts with sweet oil and remove by washing; petroleum or kerosene rubbed on two successive nights and washed each morning; vinegar to attack nits; combing daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: kerosene treatment requires avoiding open flames. Alternative: cold infusion of larkspur seed (poisonous) steeped and applied twice, then shampoo after 24 hours. Continue combing for a week for nits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothes lice — treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothes lice live in clothing and infest filthy persons; treatment is simply cleanliness of the body and clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove and wash or disinfect clothing; maintain personal hygiene to prevent reinfestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crab (pubic) lice treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Crab lice inhabit coarse hair in the genital region and nearby areas. Application of kerosene to the part is sufficient to kill the lice, but must be repeated at intervals (about a week) to kill subsequently hatched parasites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat treatments and hygiene measures; take care with kerosene and fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flea bite recognition and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Flea bites produce itching and small red points, sometimes raised lumps in children. Fleas lay eggs in cracks in floors and on dirty clothes; adult fleas leave the host after feeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control by removing environmental breeding sites (cleaning floors, washing clothing). Dog fleas are a distinct species and do not permanently infest humans; ease of eliminating fleas once environment addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jigger / sand flea removal and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: The female jigger bores into the skin (commonly near toenails), lays eggs under the skin producing itching then pain. Remove the insect with a red-hot needle or wait until it detaches; the negro (folk) method peels skin and squeezes out eggs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevention: sound shoes and regular inspection of the feet. If sores result or the insect is pressed into skin in removal attempts, serious inflammation can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housefly control to prevent disease transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The common housefly conveys disease germs (typhoid, cholera) from bowel discharges to food; flies have been a source of sickness in military camps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control measures for biting flies (sandfly, gadfly, horsefly) are similar to mosquito prevention and repellents; focus on sanitation and preventing access to food and waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorpion and centipede sting first aid
rubrics_metrics.description: First Aid Rule: Squeeze lemon juice on wound. Bathing with a two percent solution of carbolic acid, with rum, or with lemon juice is indicated to relieve the stings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stings are rarely dangerous except in young children or the feeble. Scorpions sting with a tail; centipedes have venomous bites. Keep wound clean; seek care if severe reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spider and tarantula bite first aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour water of ammonia on the bite. If the patient is depressed by the poison, give strong coffee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most trapdoor/tarantula bites are not usually dangerous though they may heal slowly. Use same remedies as for mosquito bites and support circulation if depressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snake bite — comprehensive first-aid rules
rubrics_metrics.description: First Aid Rules (summarized): (1) Make the wound bleed by cutting a lengthwise slit through the wound; DO NOT SUCK THE WOUND. (2) Keep poison out of circulation: tie a cord or bandage tightly between wound and heart, loosening every 15 minutes. (3) Use antidote: wash wound and cut with fresh solution of chloride of lime (1:60); inject anti-venene (10 cc) or permanganate solution into wound or tissues. (4) Support heart if weak: inject small doses of strychnine hypodermically as indicated. (5) Give no whisky or other liquor; do not burn the wound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other guidance: encourage bleeding and remove tissue around the wound if possible (knife excision); Rambaud recommends thorough washing with chloride of lime and forbids burning. Anti-venom serum (Calmette's) is effective for many species; a prophylactic schedule is recommended for those entering infested areas. Symptoms include local pain, swelling, discoloration, systemic nervous depression, and respiratory/cardiac compromise. Time is critical: serum/hypodermic use advised within ~80–90 minutes. Species differences and identification tips (pit viper characteristics) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dog and cat bite first aid (rabies/hydrophobia concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: First Aid Rules: (1) Make sure the animal is mad and, if suspected, send patient to a Pasteur institute if accessible. (2) Remove poison from wound: encourage bleeding by squeezing tissue; suck wound if no lip cracks and spit out fluid; pour hot carbolic solution into wound (1/3 tsp carbolic acid to a pint of hot water). (3) Cauterize: nitric acid on a wooden skewer or red-hot poker/nail or red coal may be used. (4) Do not kill the animal; if it is alive and well after a week it was not mad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referral to Pasteur institute for rabies prophylaxis is emphasized. Prompt cleansing and discouraging killing the animal (so it can be observed) are noted. These are older historical measures; definitive modern rabies prophylaxis is via Pasteur/medical facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for slight burns and scalds
rubrics_metrics.description: If slight: skin very red, unbroken. First Aid Rule: Cover with cloths wet in strong solution of baking soda in cold water. Dry gently, and spread with thick white of egg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate immersion in cold water also relieves first-degree burns. Anything protecting burned skin from air (starch, flour, molasses, white paint, egg + oil) can be used in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for deeper burns (blisters and partial-thickness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If deeper with blisters: First Aid Rule 1 — Stop pain quickly: cut away clothing gently, break no blisters, cover with Carron oil (equal parts limewater and linseed/olive oil) and light bandage; give laudanum (15 drops every half hour up to three doses). Rule 2 — Combat shock: if cold/weak/confused give a tablespoonful of whisky in hot water and place hot-water bottles at feet. Rule 3 — Quench thirst with pieces of ice in mouth or a swallow of cold milk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disturb blisters unless large/tense; support systemic condition (shock) and control pain. Follow-up wound care guidance for dressings and antiseptic measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burn classification and treatment for severe burns
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns are divided into first, second, and third classes with progressively deeper tissue damage. Severe burns (third class) may require surgical care. Immediate care: keep patient warm, cut clothing away carefully, control pain (laudanum), liquid diet, daily rectal bowel care, keep blisters intact when possible. For denuded skin use boric acid and vaseline ointment; change dressings only every 2–3 days unless discharge/odor present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very extensive burns, immersion in warm salt solution (1 tsp salt per quart; bath temp 94–104°F) covering body except head is described as comfortable and favorable to healing; maintain cleanliness, sterilize cloths by boiling and oven-drying, and avoid frequent painful dressing changes. Aftercare may involve surgical interventions like skin grafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burn by strong acid — neutralization and care
rubrics_metrics.description: First Aid Rule 1 — Neutralize the acid: scatter baking soda thickly over burn, or pour limewater over it. Rule 2 — Control pain: wash off soda with stream of water, apply Carron oil and bandage lightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If acids are the cause, initially do not wash until a mild alkali (chalk, whiting, baking soda) is sprinkled to neutralize; then wash. Apply boric-acid ointment for broken skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burn by strong alkali — neutralization and care
rubrics_metrics.description: For burns by strong alkali (ammonia, quicklime, lye): First Aid Rule 1 — Neutralize the alkali by pouring vinegar over the burn. Rule 2 — Control pain: wash off vinegar with stream of water, dry gently, apply vaseline or cold cream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For eye exposure to alkalies, dilute vinegar with three parts water before irrigation. Follow with soothing oily agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment for mineral-acid or alkali eye exposures
rubrics_metrics.description: Limewater is useful in counteracting the effect of acids spattered in the eye. In the case of alkalies in the eye, the vinegar used should be diluted with three parts water. Albolene or liquid vaseline is the best agent to drop in the eye after either accident, and the patient should stay in a dark room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt irrigation with the appropriate neutralizing solution in diluted form is emphasized; protect the eye and seek medical help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frostbite (real freezing) — staged rewarming and resuscitation
rubrics_metrics.description: First Aid Rule 1 — Restore circulation: rub gently, then vigorously, with snow. Rule 2 — Restore heat very gradually: sudden heat is fatal; keep in cold room, rub with cloth wet with very cold water until circulation established, then rub with equal parts alcohol and water and expose gradually to room heat. Rule 3 — If person ceases to breathe, resuscitate as if drowned with described manual methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply sudden warmth. The resuscitation method involves tongue control, sequential arm manipulation to expand chest, and rhythmic compressions/expansions to imitate breathing; repeat 12–15 times per minute as directed for adults, more gently for children.
